title: Giving Feedback by Asking for Help
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A companion piece to the prior day's article, this one flips the framing: instead of offering help, the leader asks the team member for help in a way that indirectly delivers the needed feedback. Using the example of a colleague who dominates group discussions, it contrasts a direct statement about talk-time dominance with an ask-for-help version that recruits the person's cooperation in getting quieter colleagues to speak up. The author argues this bookend strategy works because people are naturally inclined to help their leader, making it effective even when other approaches have failed. It's positioned as especially useful with team members who lack self-awareness about their impact on others.
points: Delivering feedback by asking for help recruits the recipient's cooperation rather than putting them on the defensive.
The technique works well precisely because team members are inclined to want to help their leader when asked directly.
It's especially effective with team members who lack self-awareness about how their behavior affects others.
Indirect feedback strategies like this one tend to be received better than direct confrontation, provided the message isn't watered down.
quotes: Giving feedback by asking for help is yet another way to offer criticism more indirectly and increase the odds that the receiving party will not feel confronted or reprimanded.
A leader could certainly deliver this feedback directly with the statement: “Your talk time versus listening time during group discussions prevents your colleagues from expressing their views.
Because team members are inclined to pitch in and help their leader, this indirect feedback strategy can work when nothing else has in the past.
Offering criticism by asking for help is especially influential with team members who lack self-awareness or are largely unaware of the impact of their behaviors on others.
Indirect feedback that doesn’t skirt the point or issue is often more effective than more direct approaches.
